presentingComplaint: Found unresponsive in a parked car with slow, shallow breathing.
history: A 29-year-old man with a known history of injection heroin use was found by a passer-by slumped in the driver's seat of a parked car, unresponsive, with visibly slow and shallow breathing. A used syringe and a foil wrapper were found nearby. Paramedics report no witnessed seizure, vomiting, or trauma. No suicide note. Friends contacted by phone report he had recently been released from a 3-week inpatient detoxification program two days prior and had "gone back to using" that evening, raising concern for reduced opioid tolerance. No history of diabetes, seizure disorder, or head injury reported. No co-ingestant packaging (e.g., benzodiazepine blister packs, alcohol bottles) identified at scene, though co-ingestion cannot be excluded.
examination: Unresponsive to verbal stimuli, responds only to painful stimuli with non-purposeful withdrawal (GCS 6: E1V1M4-ish/ approx 6). Cyanotic lips. Bilaterally pinpoint (miosis), poorly reactive pupils. Respiratory rate markedly reduced with shallow, irregular breaths; occasional apneic pauses. Skin cool, no diaphoresis. Old and fresh needle track marks over both antecubital fossae. Chest clear to auscultation, no wheeze or crepitations. Heart sounds normal, bradycardic. Abdomen soft, non-tender. No focal neurological deficits elicitable given depressed consciousness. No signs of trauma.
imaging: Chest X-ray: no infiltrate, no aspiration changes; normal cardiac silhouette
CT head (performed given depressed GCS): no acute intracranial abnormality
differentialDiagnoses: Hypercapnic respiratory failure from other cause (e.g., CNS depressant polydrug use)
finalDiagnosis: Opioid overdose with respiratory depression and miosis
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e — Opioid Poisoning and Withdrawal
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e — Approach to the Patient with Coma
contraindications: Avoid flumazenil empirically if benzodiazepine co-ingestion suspected in an opioid-dependent patient, as it can precipitate seizures
Use lowest effective naloxone dose/titration in known chronic opioid users to avoid precipitating acute severe withdrawal
Avoid physical/mechanical restraint without adequate airway management in a patient with depressed respiratory drive
edgeCases: Recent detoxification/abstinence markedly reduces opioid tolerance, increasing overdose risk at previously-tolerated doses
Long-acting or high-potency opioids (e.g., fentanyl, methadone) may require repeat or infusion naloxone dosing due to duration mismatch (naloxone half-life shorter than opioid)
Co-ingestion with benzodiazepines or alcohol is common and may blunt response to naloxone alone / worsen respiratory depression
Naloxone may only partially reverse mixed overdoses (e.g., with GABAergic agents), so a normal mental status is not guaranteed
